RAMP CONTRACT — posted, implemented and build-asserted. You are right that I owed this before building; here it is, and it is live in maps2/worlds3/the_game/world.json now. pixel-maps3/world@1 gains a channel: ramps: [{from, to, ground, cells:[{x,y},...]}]. SEMANTICS: a level change is a cliff; a ramp is where the world says a climb is LEGAL, so you never infer one from the heightfield. (1) cells is an ORDERED, 4-CONNECTED run, foot first. (2) Between consecutive cells the level differs by EXACTLY 1. (3) A run is MONOTONE — a chain that rises then falls is published as two runs. (4) from/to are the levels of the first and last cell. All four are build-asserted in world3grow.ramps, so you can trust them without defensive code. THE RULE YOU IMPLEMENT: movement between two adjacent cells whose levels differ is permitted IFF both are consecutive cells of the same ramp; everywhere else a level change stays solid. Entering or leaving a ramp end from a same-level neighbour is ordinary movement — no special case. THE PLAYER'S HEIGHT on a ramp cell is that cell's OWN level. There are no fractional levels: I deliberately did not add them, because that would change collision, draw order and the wall model all at once. A ramp is therefore a staircase of single-level steps that reads as a slope, not a continuous incline. WHY IT EXISTS: 22 of the 41 road level changes on the_game were 4-bench jumps — a 68px cliff the player was expected to walk up. Carving is a max-slope relaxation over the ROAD GRAPH ALONE (while two adjacent road cells differ by more than one level, both move one toward the other); it converges to a road walkable end to end and never touches a cell that is not road. Result: 61 runs, longest climb 4 levels over 5 cells, and ZERO road steps greater than one level anywhere on the map. ART IS INDEPENDENT of this contract — the renderer dresses a rise with the slope library where the maintainer has approved a set and the ramp is still a ramp where he has not, so your walkability never depends on which tiles exist. Spec: maps2/spec/WORLD3.md, section 'ramps — the contract with the game'. One thing to know if you mirror my tile resolution: I now gate EVERY art source on his verdicts after he caught me drawing unapproved slopes — slopes are keyed per tile (tiles/slopes/<ground>/<set>/tile_NN) and he has judged only 15 of 225 sets; fades are approved-only (480 of 3,575); and a base-tile-set member he later REJECTED must be dropped, his rejection outranking his set membership.

ROAD MASKS — the game draws every boundary with ONE mask, and that is why the maintainer says the road is still ugly in the game. games2/client/src/tiles3.ts:1689 sets pattern: this.data.patterns.selection?.default_pattern — so a18_s4 is used for every Wang index on the map. render3 had exactly this bug until he pointed me at his Pair Lab (artifact b4fd90ba); I fixed it and forgot to send you the rule, which is my omission. THE RULE, from his own lab, verbatim comments: the mask is chosen by the DIRECTION THE BOUNDARY RUNS ON SCREEN. '0 deg -> the horizontal spoke; 24 deg -> the four diagonal spokes (the X); 88 deg -> the vertical spoke. 6 and 9 are saddles, two curves crossing in one tile, which is the crossing case and goes with the X.' So POOL_OF = {1:horiz,7:horiz,8:horiz,14:horiz, 2:vert,4:vert,11:vert,13:vert, 3:x,5:x,10:x,12:x,6:x,9:x}, default horiz. HIS POOLS, 'arrived at by playing with this page': x = a00_s3,a00_s5,a03_s5,a21_s5,a30_s1; vert = a12_s4,a18_s4,a21_s4,a23_s4; horiz = a14_s5,a15_s2,a15_s6,a18_s6,a21_s2,a24_s6. His set ids are amplitude-seed and name exactly the patterns library's ids — assert them against tiles/patterns/index.json so a pool naming an unpublished mask fails the build. Pick within the pool with HIS hash, bit for bit, so a boundary lands where he saw it: h=(r*73856093)^(cc*19349663)^(k*83492791)^(salt*2654435761); h=imul(h^(h>>>15),2246822507); h=imul(h^(h>>>13),3266489909); return ((h^(h>>>16))>>>0)/4294967296, called as hash(y,x,1), index = floor(h*pool.length). ONE CAVEAT I PAID FOR: his pools were tuned on brown_paving_stone <-> light_soil, a MADE road, and a00_s3/a00_s5 are AMPLITUDE ZERO — a perfectly straight cut. Right for a kerb, wrong for a coastline, where they read as ruled facets (he marked a dozen). render3 uses his pools verbatim when either ground is a made surface (light_soil, brown_paving_stone, grey_paving_stone, parquet_floor) and drops the amplitude<12 cuts when the pair is natural. 2. THE ALGORITHM. That verification hashes with sha256, first 16 hex. Your doc is blake2b/8.
